Could anyone explain to me why this is happening? Also, I am curious how I can actually approach the prior predictive distribution once the argument works.

I attach the code I used:

library(blavaan)
library(rstan)
options(mc.cores = 2)

model <- ' 
    # latent variable definitions
    ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4
    dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8
     
    # regressions
    dem60 ~ ind60
    dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
     
    # residual correlations
    y1 ~~ y5
    y2 ~~ y4 + y6
    y3 ~~ y7
    y4 ~~ y8
    y6 ~~ y8
'

fit <- bsem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy, n.chains = 2, prisamp = TRUE,
            burnin = 2500, sample = 2500)
summary(fit)

Thanks!

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Using prisamp gives me long and iterative errors
parts:
Hi Ihnwhi,

For the particular model that you are using, there is a funny covariance matrix (some off-diagonal zeros and some off-diagonal free parameters). blavaan puts a separate prior on each individual correlation here, which can lead to a non-positive definite covariance matrix. Some further discussion can be found in Sec 5.2 here:

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07733.pdf

I am currently looking at a solution to this. If you remove the residual correlations from the model, those errors should go away.

But once you get the "fit" object, you should be able to use all the blavaan commands as if you had sampled from the posterior. For example, if you want a list of all the draws, you can do something like

blavInspect(fit, 'mcmc')

Ed

Last additional question, please. I am considering the possibilities of using the prior predictive samples to evaluate the marginal likelihoods with the bridge sampling package. This should still be the prior model. It depends on the data that is being passed in to Stan (the data that is exported with mcmcfile=TRUE). In that data, there are two binary integers: has_data and has_cov. If both equal 0, then you get samples from the prior.

Ed

One update and one question about this thread.

1. I posted an issue on the Stan discourse (https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/how-does-stan-work-during-warm-up-stan-warm-up-algorithm-stan-burn-in-algorithm/19690). Following your recommendations, it seems safe to set the burn-in samples.

2. I am wondering whether there are additional changes in the semstan.rda file other than has_cov = 0 and has_data = 0. I tried to compare the estimates of the log marginal likelihood between the Laplace approximation (blavaan) and bridge sampler (bridge sampling). I used the code below:

library(blavaan)
library(rstan)
options(mc.cores = 1)
library(bridgesampling)

model.consideration <- '
# measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions
dem60 ~ ind60
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60

'

set.seed(1)
blav.fit <- bsem(model.consideration, data=PoliticalDemocracy, n.chains = 2, prisamp = TRUE,
                 burnin = 5000, sample = 5000, mcmcfile = 'prior-check/ppp-2', do.fit=TRUE)
summary(blav.fit) # LogML from Laplace approximation: -3153.237

load('prior-check/ppp-2/semstan.rda')
set.seed(1)
stan.fit <- stan('prior-check/ppp-2/sem.stan', data=stantrans$data, init = stantrans$inits,
                 chains=2, iter=10000, warmup = 5000)

set.seed(1)
bridge_sampler(stan.fit) # LogML from bridge sampler: 0.01426

From the blavaan object, the log marginal likelihood (Laplace approximation) is -3153.237. On the other hand, the log marginal likelihood from the bridge sampling is 0.014. When I try the same after setting the prisamp argument to FALSE (i.e., posterior samples), the estimates are close to each other. Can has_cov = 0 and has_data = 0 in the semstan.rda have tremendous effects on this differing log marginal likelihood estimate? If there are other possibilities, I would like to know the origin of this difference. Also, can I only extract the log marginal likelihood from the Laplace approximation in blavaan with the blavInspect() function? I tried to find it but could not.

Best,
Ihnwhi

parts:
Hi Ihnwhi,

I think it might help to step away from the code for a minute and consider the general procedure. We want to randomly generate parameters from the prior, and those parameters should not be involved in the log-likelihood calculation (in "target"). So the "target +=" part of the priors needs to change. Basically, instead of declaring all the model parameters in the "parameters" block, you are drawing them using the rng functions. Instead of "target +=", you are using names of the parameters from the parameters block, and then deleting the declarations from the parameters block. This is somewhat similar to what happens in simulation-based calibration (via the rstan function sbc()).

You will probably have to play with where the _rng commands are located. For example, they might have to go in transformed data instead of transformed parameters, and subsequent commands in those blocks will depend on the _rng commands. And I might be forgetting other details, but this is the general idea!

Ed
